options: Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.explanation: Every (a,a) is present, so R is reflexive, and each off-diagonal pair appears with its reverse, so R is symmetric. But (1,2) and (2,3) are in R while (1,3) is not, so R is not transitive.

questions.q: The principal value of cos⁻¹(cos(7π/6)) is:
questions.explanation: The range of cos⁻¹ is [0, π]. Since 7π/6 lies outside it, use cos(7π/6) = cos(2π − 7π/6) = cos(5π/6), and 5π/6 is in [0, π]. So the value is 5π/6.

questions.q: If A is a 3×3 matrix with |A| = 4, then |2A| equals:
questions.explanation: For an n×n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|. Here n = 3, so |2A| = 2³ × 4 = 8 × 4 = 32.

questions.q: If the points (2, −3), (k, 2) and (−1, 4) are collinear, then k equals:
questions.explanation: Collinear points give a zero-area determinant: x₁(y₂−y₃) + x₂(y₃−y₁) + x₃(y₁−y₂) = 0. So 2(2−4) + k(4−(−3)) + (−1)((−3)−2) = −4 + 7k + 5 = 0 → 7k = −1 → k = −1/7.

questions.q: The value of k that makes f(x) = kx² for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 3 for x > 2 continuous at x = 2 is:
questions.explanation: For continuity at x = 2, the left limit must equal the right limit: k(2)² = 3 → 4k = 3 → k = 3/4.
The numerator 2x is exactly the derivative of the denominator 1 + x². An integral of the form ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C, so the answer is log|1 + x²| + C.

questions.q: The order and degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁵ + y = 0 are:
questions.explanation: Order is the highest derivative present — here d²y/dx², so order 2. Degree is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is polynomial in derivatives — here it is cubed, so degree 3.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled. Given that the number is odd, the probability it is prime is:
questions.explanation: Odd outcomes are {1, 3, 5}. Among these the primes are 3 and 5. By conditional probability, P(prime | odd) = 2/3.

faq.q: Which Class 12 Maths chapters carry the most marks in the board exam?
faq.a: Calculus dominates — integrals, application of derivatives, continuity and differentiability, and differential equations together account for the largest weightage. Vectors, three-dimensional geometry, matrices and determinants, and probability follow. Prioritise these when time is short.

faq.q: How are 'important questions' different from just solving the NCERT textbook?
faq.a: Important questions are the sums examiners repeat year after year — NCERT exercises, exemplar problems and past-paper favourites filtered down to the highest-yield ones. NCERT is the base; important questions tell you where to concentrate revision.

faq.q: How should I revise chapter-wise in the final month?
faq.a: Take one chapter per study block, revise its formulas, then solve 8 to 10 mixed important questions from it without looking at solutions. Mark the ones you miss and redo only those two days later. This spaced approach beats re-reading.

faq.q: Are inverse trigonometry and determinants worth the effort for their few marks?
faq.a: Yes. Both are short, formula-driven chapters where the questions are predictable, so the marks are almost guaranteed once you drill the principal-value ranges and the property-based determinant shortcuts. They protect your score with little study time.
